exa.title: How to secure your account with two-factor authentication (2FA) | Kraken
exa.snippet:
Last updated: October 13, 2026

Two-factor authentication (2FA), sometimes called multi-factor authentication (MFA), adds a second check to your Kraken account on top of your password. If someone gets hold of your password, they still can’t sign in without your 2FA.

Kraken supports two 2FA methods: Passkeys and authenticator apps. We recommend a Passkey wherever you can use one.

2FA with a Passkey (recommended)

Passkeys are our recommended 2FA method because they’re phishing-resistant, thanks to FIDO2 technology. A Passkey can be a Hardware Security Key, a Cross-Device Passkey (created on a mobile device or linked to a keychain or password manager, such as iCloud Keychain or 1Password), or a Device-Bound Passkey (unique to one browser on one device). Which options you’re offered depends on your device, browser and operating system. See What is a Passkey?

You can use a Passkey for Sign-in 2FA and for your Master Key.

### Why use a Passkey?

- Simplicity You confirm your identity the way you already unlock your device, or touch your Hardware Security Key. There’s no code to copy.
- Security Passkeys use public-key cryptography and only work on Kraken’s real site, so they can’t be phished or reused on a fake site the way a typed code can.
- Privacy Kraken never sees or stores your Passkey.

2FA with an authenticator app

An authenticator app is usually installed on a smartphone and generates a 6 to 8 digit code every 30 seconds. You can use one for Sign-in 2FA, Master Key, Funding 2FA and Trading 2FA.

For Sign-in 2FA and your Master Key, if you choose an authenticator app instead of a Passkey, be aware of the risks. Its codes can be entered on a phishing website or shared with a scammer, and codes synced to a Google, Apple or Microsoft account are exposed if that account is compromised. See Risks of using an authenticator app.

What are the 2FA functions?

Each function has its own 2FA and is set up separately: Sign-in 2FA, Master Key, Funding 2FA and Trading 2FA

## The security hierarchy for a crypto exchange  
Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second proof of identity after your password. The quality of that second factor depends on whether an attacker can copy it remotely, trick you into revealing it, or take over the account used to receive it.  
1. **FIDO2/WebAuthn security key:**best choice when supported. The credential is held by a physical key and authentication is bound to the legitimate website.

5. **Backup codes:**emergency recovery material, not a replacement for a primary authenticator.

This guide explains the security features that separate a safe exchange from a risky one, the red flags to watch for, how to spot a fake platform, and how to protect your own account.
A platform with low fees and a huge coin list can still fail our security assessment if it stores customer funds carelessly or offers weak account protection. When we evaluate how safe a crypto exchange is, we look at: Custody setup: How much of customer funds the exchange keeps in cold storage, and whether it uses multisignature or multi-party computation (MPC) wallets so no single person or key can move funds. Account protection options: Which two-factor authentication methods it supports, whether it offers phishing-resistant options such as hardware security keys and passkeys, and whether it provides withdrawal allowlists and anti-phishing codes.
Without encryption on every page, your login details and financial information can be intercepted in transit. Missing basics raise the risk of account takeovers, data breaches, and identity theft. They also say a lot about how the exchange treats security behind the scenes.
The safest crypto exchanges go further with withdrawal allowlists, regular independent security audits, and phishing-resistant login options.
